title: Boardspeak - See the tools your agent can use (in a game!)
pitch: An AI agent has 2 bad options for using a website: screenshot and guess or a separate MCP server. WebMCP is the 3rd way: the page itself tells you what you can do. Boardspeak is that, as a board game
about_excerpt: An AI agent has 2 bad options for using a website: screenshot and guess or a separate MCP server. WebMCP is the 3rd way: the page itself tells you what you can do. Boardspeak is that, as a board game Like Comment Story Updates agent plays boardspeak codex agent tools agent call trace Inspiration Today, an AI agent has 2 bad options for using websites: 1) it can take screenshots and guess or 2) the website owner can build a separate “MCP server” that the AI talks to instead of the website. WebMCP is a third way: the web page itself says, in plain JS, “here are the things you can do here and here’s exactly how” - that’s super powerful, especially if we imagine a future where AI does more for us. The specification names improving accessibility through agents as an explicit goal, and I wanted to test that goal on something pretty complex. A board game is the hardest thing I could think of in time for this challenge - the state is entirely visual, legality changes every single turn, and both players have to be looking at the same board state or it's not a game. What it does Boardspeak plays Breakthrough (Dan Troyka, 2000). 8x8, pawns only and pretty simple rules - get your pawn to the other side of the board, you can only go forward (diagonals+straight), and you can eat enemy pawns diagonally. In our scenario, White plays by mouse (a person, or the built-in bot if you're alone) and Black plays by talking or typing to the agent. The page publishes the live board to the agent as 9 WebMCP tools. Ask "what's on the board?" or "what's threatening my left flank?" and the answer comes from the game itself, not from a screenshot. Say "advance the pawn on e7" and the piece moves on the shared board state. Tools appear and disappear with the position. play_capture exists only while a capture is available. list_threats exists only while a pawn is one step from its goal rank. suggest_move exists only on the human's turn, and play_move only on the agent's. An agent that inspects this page mid-game sees a different set of tools than it saw 30 seconds ago, and that set is always exactly what is legal right now. An agent steering a game is not the new part; 2 players and an agent sharing one adversarial board, with the schema as the rulebook, is, and that's the really cool thing that WebMCP enables. Every agent call is logged on the page with its arguments and its result, so both players can see what happened without opening DevTools. The game is fully playable by mouse, in any browser, with no agent and no API key. In Chrome, Black can even play by voice with no agent at all: an on-page mic takes moves like "a7 to a6" and matches them against the same legal-move list, and saying "options" reads the legal moves out loud....but to play by talking to an agent you'll need ChatGPT's or Codex's built-in browser, or Chrome with the WebMCP flag! How I built it The idea: legality isn't checked inside the tool. The tool only offers legal moves in the first place. For example, play_move 's input schema is regenerated every turn to enumerate exactly the legal moves, so a schema-respecting client can't even form an illegal move. The schema is the contract so a client that ignores it meets the engine, which refuses anything outside of those rules and tells the agent why. I built this on Next.js 15 on Vercel. The game keeps no state on any server and there is no database; the only server code is the optional narration route (works without a key). One bridge component registers each tool on document.modelContext through GoogleChromeLabs' use-webmcp-tool hook, each with its own AbortController - a turn change aborts the old registration and registers the new one. The piece I am most happy about is the commit barrier. No mutating tool call resolves until React has committed the new board and the new tool surface, so that the agent's next getTools already reflects the move it just made and there is no moment where the screen and the agent can even disagree. Tool calls are serialized through a queue so 2 calls cannot interleave mid-turn. readOnlyHint is set on every read tool. Mutating tools return the full board text so the agent can verify what happened rather than assume. resign_game and start_new_game wait on an in-page confirmation. The page draws its own "are you sure?" dialog and waits for a real click, because the protocol does not have a built-in way to ask the human yet. Challenges I ran into WebMCP can't edit a tool after it's registered, and it refuses a second tool with the same name. So every turn the page has to remove the old move tool before adding the new one, in exactly that order, or it crashes mid-game. I wrote a test that plays 20 moves plus a full game reset against a fake browser that throws the moment any tool name repeats, and it finishes with zero errors. The other hard part was resisting the urge to make the agent the star. Every time I gave it a more powerful tool, the game got worse. suggest_move exists because the version where the agent could move the human's pieces was not fun to play against. Two limits I kept instead of hiding. The size check on tool responses runs before the board updates for the two move tools only; the others check after, which is fine today because their responses are small, but it is not the same guarantee. And the "are you sure?" step is a dialog my page draws itself, because the protocol does not have a built-in one yet. I would rather say that than pretend it does. Accomplishments that I'm proud of 9 tools that come and go with the position, so an illegal move is not even a choice the agent can make 82 unit tests, 9 full browser tests from a clean install, and 5 of 5 WebMCP eval cases A perfect 100 Lighthouse accessibility score on mobile and desktop, with the report in the repo Fully playable by mouse in any browser, no agent, no flag, no API key A live panel showing the agent's current tools, and you can watch it change as you play 2 people and an agent on one board, and the board + agent are fully aligned What I learned The list of tools a page offers does not have to be fixed. Publishing exactly what is legal right now, and nothing else, is the most useful thing a page can tell an agent. And it goes way past games: forms, wizards, checkout flows, anything with steps and rules. The harder lesson: the interesting question in building for agents is not what to expose. It is what to withhold, and when. What's next for Boardspeak Both colors by voice, with two agents sharing one board. More games behind the same engine contract. And a getTools -driven spectator mode, where a third agent can watch without being able to touch anything.
